To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

the formation of cell assemblies in a neurocomputational architecture with neuroanatomically constrained connectivity leads to a mechanism for long-term memory of sensorimotor associations, and that persistent activity in the cell assembly neurons in multimodal areas provides a mechanism for the "disembodiments" of working memory.
the formation of distributed cell assembly structures, including those of working memory, is a consequence of sensorimotor learning and neuroanatomical network structure.
the emergence of memory cells in higher association areas is a result of sensorimotor learning, and the neuroanatomical connectivity pattern of the model networks is a key factor in this process.
In summary, our research is concerned with

how sensorimotor learning leads to formation of cell assembly-based memory circuits in frontotemporo-cortical areas, and how these circuits provide the neurocomputational basis for long-term and working memory.
the neurobiological basis of memory formation and its relation to working memory.
the neurocomputational mechanisms underlying the formation of memory cells in higher association cortex and their functional role in working memory.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that

disembodiment of memory cells in higher association areas is a consequence of sensorimotor learning, which leads to the emergence of distributed cell assemblies, and of the neuroanatomical architecture of the brain. (PsycINFO Database Record (c) 2019 APA, all rights reserved)
the neurocomputational simulations presented here show how sensorimotor learning leads to the emergence of working memory cells in multimodal association cortices.
memory cells in pre- frontal and temporal association cortex are the result of sensorimotor learning in the brain.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the formation of cell assemblies in the brain is a mechanism for the storage of information in memory and that this process is a fundamental principle of the brain's operation.
we show how sensorimotor learning leads to memory cell formation in multimodal association areas, thus explaining the "disembodiments" of memory.
memory cells are not a special type of neurons, but rather that they are neurons with special functions.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the emergence of disembodiment is a natural outcome of neuroplasticity in the context of a neurocomputational architecture that is consistent with the neuroanatomy of the brain.
the neurocomputational modelling framework we used can provide insights into the neural mechanisms underlying memory formation and maintenance.
memory cells are formed in distributed circuits that include multimodal association areas, which are distant from sensorimotor areas.
